To see which theory can do without an ultraviolet (high-energy) regulator, recall why regularization is introduced in the first place: loop integrals (or classical self-energies) typically diverge at short distances / high energies.  

A. Quantum Chromodynamics – Although QCD is asymptotically free, perturbative loop integrals still have ultraviolet divergences; dimensional or lattice regularization is routinely used.  

B. Classical Electrodynamics – The self-energy of a point charge diverges as r→0, so some cutoff or other regularization is needed to keep the theory sensible.  

C. Quantum Electrodynamics – Standard example of a theory that requires UV regularization (Pauli–Villars, dimensional, etc.) before renormalization.  

D. Superstring Theory – Because fundamental objects are extended strings, interactions are smeared over a finite length (the string length). This softens short-distance behavior so that perturbative amplitudes stay finite; no separate high-energy regulator is required. Superstring theory is therefore considered ultraviolet-finite (at least perturbatively) and does not need regularization the way point-particle field theories do.

Hence only option (D) fits.

Answer: D
